newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium streaks higher by end of PM kerb.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium streaks higher by end of PM kerb.

text.p: Aluminium was a star performer on Monday, extending gains and breaking above nearby resistance, but copper made only modest progress despite wide spreads.
Three months aluminium touched the highest price in nearly eight months, peaking at $1,625 a tonne and equalling the high on May 20, 1996.
The market finished the afternoon kerb $28 higher at $1,624 per tonne just above a band of resistance pegged at $1,615/20.
"It is now back above the original trendline from the October low, which shows it is keeping up its momentum," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff.

"The next bit of resistance is around $1,638/40 with the target at $1,680. But we will not get there unless the LME stocks start falling," he said, adding it was possible that inventories could fall slightly on Tuesday.
LME stocks rose on Friday by 9,375 tonnes, but IPAI producer stocks fell further in November to a four-year low.
"The stocks/consumption ratio is now nine weeks, just two weeks or 600,000 tonnes away from critical," Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group said in a commentary.
Copper spreads flared on Monday, reacting to Third Wednesday pricing, but three months prices barely followed suit.
The premium of cash over three months metal ended at around $185, up about $35 from Friday, with the premium over February at about $130, accounting for a good deal of the tightness.
Three months copper, however, only edged up by $8 to $2,263, reflecting the mixed views on LME stocks data.
Predictions ranged from slightly up to slightly down after a decline of 3,425 tonnes on Friday and a rise on last Tuesday.
"Over the next month there's still the potential for more tightness and another $150 to $200 on three months," Adams said.
"It's important, however, not to forget that supply will tend to start catching up," he added.
Producers were likely to take advantage of rising prices for hedging purposes.
Tin broke out of a sideways pattern, adding $100 to $5,960, with the next target at the December 9 high of $6,015.
The market has been concerned that heavy exporting by the Chinese would lead to that metal showing up in LME stocks, but that fear was probably already in the price, Adams said.
Nickel ended unchanged at $7,200, showing resilience after dipping $100 during the day to explore lower territory.
Lead shed $6 to $692, zinc added $6 to $1,070 and alloy rose to $1,521/25 from $1,515.
